cues.text: A Church Torn Over the Nature of Christ

In the early fourth century, a priest of Alexandria named Arius began teaching that the Son of God was a creature — the first and greatest of God's creations, but not eternal and not equal to the Father in substance.
To Arius, there was a time when the Son "was not."
His bishop, Alexander of Alexandria , condemned the teaching and excommunicated him around 320.
Arius found sympathizers among influential bishops in the East, and the controversy spread through the recently Christianized Roman Empire with startling speed.
Arius framed his teaching in catchy, singable verse — a collection called the Thalia — that made his ideas easy to spread among ordinary Christians, sailors, and merchants, not just theologians.
Within a few years, disputes over the Son's status were reportedly breaking out in marketplaces and public baths across the eastern Mediterranean.
This was an early sign of how deeply doctrinal questions had become bound up with the everyday life of the newly tolerated Church.
Emperor Constantine , who had legalized Christianity only a decade earlier with the Edict of Milan, saw the dispute as a threat to the unity he was trying to build.

An early letter urging Alexander and Arius to reconcile over what he considered a minor disagreement went nowhere; it was becoming clear this was no small quarrel but a fundamental question about who Christ was.
Constantine Convenes a Council
Rather than let the crisis fester, Constantine summoned bishops from across the Christian world to meet at Nicaea in Bithynia.
The city, in modern-day İznik, Turkey, offered accessibility by both land and sea and proximity to his own residence at Nicomedia.
The council opened in the summer of 325 and is traditionally counted as the first ecumenical council of the Church.
Accounts vary on the exact number present, but tradition settled on 318 bishops , a figure echoing the number of Abraham's servants in Genesis 14 and later given symbolic weight by Church writers.
Pope St. Sylvester I , too elderly to travel, sent legates, including Hosius of Cordova , who is thought to have presided in the pope's name.
Constantine himself opened the proceedings and took an active, if non-voting, interest throughout.
Debating a Single Word
The council's central task was to find language that could exclude Arius's teaching without ambiguity.
Various formulas were proposed and rejected as too easily reconciled with Arian belief.
The bishops eventually settled on the Greek term homoousios — "of one substance" or "consubstantial" — to describe the Son's relationship to the Father.
The word was not found in Scripture but was judged necessary to close every loophole Arian sympathizers might exploit.
The resulting Nicene Creed declared the Son "true God of true God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father."
Arius and two bishops who refused to sign, Theonas and Secundus, were excommunicated and exiled.
Constantine also ordered Arius's writings burned, effectively making the dispute a matter of imperial as well as ecclesiastical concern.
Other Business of the Council
Beyond the Creed, the bishops at Nicaea addressed a number of disciplinary matters through twenty canons.
Among the most significant: Fixing a uniform, universal date for the celebration of Easter , independent of the Jewish calendar.
This ended a long-running dispute known as the Quartodeciman controversy.
Regulating the ordination of clergy who had lapsed during the recent persecutions.
Establishing rules on clerical discipline and the authority of metropolitan bishops over their provinces.
Recognizing the traditional honor and jurisdiction of the sees of Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch.
The council closed with a banquet Constantine held to mark the twentieth anniversary of his reign, at which he urged the assembled bishops toward continued unity.
Legacy
Nicaea did not end Arianism; the controversy raged on for decades.
Several of Constantine's imperial successors — including his own son Constantius II — favored Arian or semi-Arian factions.
At times, they exiled the very bishops who had defended Nicene orthodoxy at the council, most famously St. Athanasius of Alexandria.
He spent years in repeated exile defending the Nicene faith almost single-handedly.
It would take another full ecumenical council, at Constantinople in 381, to secure the Nicene position decisively.
But the council fixed the theological vocabulary — homoousios above all — that Catholic orthodoxy would use to defend Christ’s full divinity for the rest of Christian history.
Its Creed, expanded at Constantinople, remains the profession of faith recited at Mass to this day.
Nicaea's fixed, universal date for Easter also gave the whole Church, for the first time, a shared liturgical calendar independent of any single local tradition.
As the first council to gather bishops from across the Christian world at imperial invitation, Nicaea also set the pattern for every ecumenical council that followed.
Each addressed a disputed question of faith, brought before the universal Church's bishops, and settled by a decision binding on the whole body of believers.
